study.title: Hebrews 4 The promised rest, the word that examines and the throne of grace
study.overview: Hebrews 4 presents a serious exhortation: the promise to enter into the rest of God remains valid, but is not received automatically. The author shows that hearing the good news without faith and obedience produces loss, as happened to the Israelites in the desert. Then he states that there is still a rest of God for his people, and that we must strive to enter into it. The chapter then deepens the warning: the word of God reaches the human interior and reveals the heart before God. Finally, the text leads to Christological consolation: because Jesus is the great High Priest who has compassion on our weaknesses, the believer can approach with confidence the throne of grace.

outline.title: The promise of rest and the danger of unbelief
outline.explanation: The author exhorts the reverent fear of the possibility of falling short of the promise. The good news was also announced to the old ones, but did not take advantage of them because it was not united with the faith and because there was disobedience. The central point is that the rest of God remains offered, but should not be treated with neglect.

outline.title: There remains a rest for the people of God
outline.explanation: The "hoje" of the Psalm shows that the voice of God continues to call, not just in the past. Had Joshua given the final rest, David would not have spoken after another day. Thus, the rest of God remains open, and the people must strive to enter it, avoiding repeating the pattern of disobedience.

outline.title: The word you judge and confident access to Christ
outline.explanation: The word of God is alive, penetrating and unmasks the intentions of the heart before God. After this warning, the author presents Jesus as the great High Priest, superior and compassionate, who opened access to the throne of grace. The right answer is to persevere in confession and to approach with confidence to receive mercy and help.

study.context: The chapter resumes the warning of the previous chapter, comparing the desert generation with the readers of the letter. The notes provided highlight that the author uses Israel's history as an example for the Christian community, showing that the simple hearing of the promise is not enough. The rest mentioned is described as a spiritual and eternal reality, linked to the relationship of covenant with God through Christ, without the text given requiring it to a single dimension. The reference to the Sabbath, Joshua and David serve to show continuity of God's purpose and the presentness of the divine call.
study.theology: Hebrews 4 teaches that the divine promise demands obedient faith. The rest of God is not only physical rest, but participation in communion with him, consummated in eschatological hope and already experienced spiritually by the believer. The chapter also affirms the effectiveness of God's word: it not only informs, but judges the interior, revealing thoughts and intentions. Therefore, Christian perseverance is not based on the very strength, but on the mediation of Jesus, who is a compassionate, sinless high priest, and who gives us confident access to the presence of God. The trust of the believer is not presumption, but faith founded on the grace and work of Christ.

scholarViews.insight: Listening to the good news is not enough; it must be combined with faith, for unbelief and disobedience prevent the entry into promised rest.
The promised rest in Christ is presented as a precious inheritance, a spiritual communion and a hope that must be assumed with seriousness.
The exhortation to enter rest emphasizes that this rest is still future for believers and should not be lost by unbelief.

questions: In what aspects does my life show that I really hear the voice of God with faith, and not just with religious knowledge?
What forms of disobedience or hardening can be turning away from the rest of God today?
Have I approached Christ with filial trust, or try to carry alone guilt, fears and weaknesses?
study.practice: This week, read Hebrews 4 in prayer and make an honest assessment of the heart in the light of verses 12 and 13. Identify a concrete area of disobedience, repent of it and ask God to obey in the present "host." Also practice the confidence of verse 16: instead of hiding from God when you fail, come near him in prayer, asking for mercy and grace for the moment of need. If possible, share with another Christian an area in which you need to persevere, so that there is mutual responsibility.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not explain in detail all the symbols of the chapter, especially the exact relationship between "repous", "sábado" and the future consummation; therefore, the synthesis above preserves the explicit emphases of the text and commentators without defining more than the material allows. There are also textual variations mentioned in Tyndale's notes in 4:2, but the main meaning remains the same: the lack was of faith before the word heard.
